name: REINFORCE with Leave-One-Out Baseline (RLOO)
key_paper: Ahmadian et al., 'Back to Basics: Revisiting REINFORCE-Style Optimization for Language Models with RLOO', ACL 2024 (also arXiv:2402.14740, February 2024)
algorithm_description: RLOO is a multi-sample REINFORCE variant that computes a separate baseline for each sample by averaging the returns of all other k-1 samples in the same batch. For k samples drawn from the policy for the same input, the gradient for sample i uses the mean return of the remaining k-1 samples as its control variate (leave-one-out baseline). This removes the need for a separate learned value network (critic), reducing parameter count and training complexity. The estimator is unbiased conditioned on the other k-1 samples and achieves lower variance than single-sample REINFORCE as k increases. Ahmadian et al. show it consistently outperforms PPO-style Actor-Critic on RLHF alignment tasks, especially when the dataset is small, because the critic does not need to be separately trained and cannot overfit.
action_space_handling: RLOO is policy-agnostic: it handles whatever action space the underlying policy defines. For discrete multi-label outputs (lottery numbers), the policy network produces logits over {1..N} and samples are drawn independently per position or autoregressively. RLOO imposes no constraints on how samples are drawn — it only wraps the sampling step with a leave-one-out averaging baseline. The k samples per input are drawn i.i.d. from the current policy.
how_combinatorial_output_is_formed: RLOO itself does not specify the combinatorial generation mechanism — it is a gradient estimator that wraps any sampling policy. For lottery-number generation, the existing policy (e.g. temperature-softmax over 50 balls, repeated 7 times with masking to enforce distinctness) would be used unchanged. The k plays generated per draw would each be a full combinatorial output; RLOO then computes the baseline across those k plays. Autoregressive masking or post-hoc rejection sampling for distinctness can be used in combination with RLOO without modification.
sequential_generation_strategy: RLOO is compatible with both joint (flat multi-hot BCEWithLogitsLoss sampling) and autoregressive generation. In the lottery-nn codebase the existing joint generation (7 independent sigmoid draws with post-hoc uniqueness enforcement) could be used as-is. For higher-quality combinatorial outputs, autoregressive masking (sample ball 1, mask it, sample ball 2 from remaining 49, etc.) pairs naturally with RLOO because each full sequence has a well-defined log-probability used in the REINFORCE score-function gradient.
gradient_estimator_type: RLOO uses the score-function (REINFORCE) gradient estimator with a leave-one-out control variate. For k samples {x_1, ..., x_k} from policy pi, the gradient for sample x_i is: grad_theta log pi(x_i) * (R(x_i) - (1/(k-1)) * sum_{j != i} R(x_j)). This is an unbiased estimator of the policy gradient with variance reduced by approximately 1/k relative to single-sample REINFORCE. No reparameterization trick is used; the estimator works directly on discrete samples. It is strictly lower-variance than vanilla REINFORCE and avoids the bias introduced by a separately-trained critic.
combinatorial_constraint_enforcement: RLOO does not itself enforce combinatorial constraints — it operates on rewards from complete plays. Constraint enforcement is delegated to the policy: autoregressive masking (most principled, exact log-prob computation), rejection sampling (simplest, but wasteful), or differentiable top-k (approximate, allows backprop but not needed since RLOO uses score-function gradients). For lottery-nn, autoregressive masking is the recommended pairing because it gives exact log-probabilities for the REINFORCE gradient.
sample_efficiency_rating: High — RLOO achieves higher sample efficiency than Actor-Critic on small datasets because it eliminates the critic network that must itself be fitted from data. With fewer than 200 training draws, a learned critic tends to overfit the value function, introducing bias that hurts policy updates. RLOO's leave-one-out baseline is computed entirely from within-batch samples, requiring no additional data. The quality of the baseline improves with k (samples per input) rather than requiring more training data, making it well-suited to the lottery-nn regime of ~100 draws per lottery.
regularization_built_in: RLOO has no built-in regularization beyond what the policy itself provides. Common additions used alongside RLOO include: (1) entropy bonus on the policy logits to prevent mode collapse (adding lambda * H[pi] to the reward), (2) KL penalty from a reference/frozen policy (used in RLHF settings), (3) gradient clipping (standard practice). For lottery-nn, an entropy bonus on the 50-ball logits is strongly recommended to maintain diversity across the k plays generated per draw.
known_failure_modes_on_small_data: 1. High variance when k is small (k=2 is near-equivalent to single-sample REINFORCE). A minimum of k=4 to k=8 samples per input is needed to get meaningful baseline quality. 2. Reward sparsity collapse: if all k plays score 0 hits in a batch, the leave-one-out baseline is 0 for all, producing zero gradient — identical to the lottery sparse-reward problem. Mitigation: use number-level (semi-bandit) credit assignment rather than play-level reward. 3. Policy collapse toward a fixed set if entropy regularization is omitted. 4. Gradient noise amplification on very small batches; mini-batch size should be at least k*num_inputs per update step.
data_regime_evidence: Ahmadian et al. (2024) validate RLOO primarily on RLHF alignment tasks (Summarize from Feedback, Anthropic HH) where training sets range from ~90K to ~300K preference pairs — much larger than the lottery-nn regime. However, the theoretical variance reduction guarantee holds for any dataset size. The key advantage over Actor-Critic becomes more pronounced as training data shrinks, because the critic's estimation error dominates at small n. Minimum training samples tested in the paper: approximately 5K-10K filtered samples. Performance at n < 200 is not directly empirically validated in the paper; the small-data advantage is inferred from the critic-free design argument. Marked uncertain for the sub-200-sample regime.
convergence_guarantees_small_n: [uncertain] RLOO inherits standard REINFORCE convergence guarantees: convergence to a local optimum under appropriate learning rate schedules (Robbins-Monro conditions). No finite-sample bounds specific to n < 200 exist in the literature. The leave-one-out baseline is unbiased (conditional on the other k-1 samples), so asymptotic convergence is preserved. In practice, convergence speed at n < 200 depends heavily on reward sparsity and the choice of k; empirical validation on lottery-scale data would be needed.
reward_distribution_handling: RLOO handles sparse reward through the leave-one-out baseline: when most plays score 0, the baseline is near 0, and any play with 1+ hits produces a positive advantage, amplifying its gradient signal. This is structurally better than a learned critic that may predict near-zero value everywhere and suppress gradients entirely. For the lottery-nn sparse reward (~95% zero-hit plays), number-level semi-bandit credit assignment (reward each of the 7 drawn numbers by how often it appears in winning draws rather than only scoring the full play) is recommended to increase signal density. Distributional returns are not natively supported but can be layered on separately.
credit_assignment_granularity: RLOO assigns credit at the play level by default (one reward R(x_i) per complete play x_i). This is the weakest form of credit assignment for lottery prediction. However, RLOO can be extended to number-level credit by defining the reward as a sum over individual ball selections: R(x_i) = sum_j r(ball_j), where r(ball_j) is the historical hit frequency of ball_j. This semi-bandit decomposition is compatible with autoregressive RLOO and significantly increases gradient signal density from ~0.05 non-zero rewards per play to up to 7 non-zero rewards per play.
diversity_mechanism: RLOO generates k plays per input in each forward pass, providing natural within-batch diversity. However, the policy may still collapse to a single mode across training steps if entropy is not regularized. Recommended mechanisms for lottery-nn: (1) entropy bonus H[pi] added to the per-ball reward, (2) within-batch diversity reward penalizing plays that duplicate balls chosen by other plays in the same batch, (3) temperature annealing starting at T>1 and reducing over training. The k=5-8 range provides reasonable diversity without excessive compute.
offline_vs_online_rl_compatibility: RLOO is an on-policy algorithm: it requires drawing fresh samples from the current policy at each update step. In the lottery-nn setting this means generating k candidate plays per historical draw date, computing their simulated reward against the actual draw result, then updating the policy. This is fully compatible with offline historical data — the 'environment' is the historical draw record, not a live draw. Each training step samples k plays, looks up the historical result for that date, and computes rewards. No live draw interaction is required. This makes RLOO highly practical for lottery-nn: one pass through the ~100 historical draws per lottery, generating k=5-8 plays per draw, gives 500-800 reward signals per epoch.
key_dependencies: PyTorch only. No additional libraries required beyond the existing lottery-nn stack. RLOO is implemented as a custom loss function (~30 lines of PyTorch). The TRL library (Hugging Face) includes a reference RLOO implementation (trl.RLOOTrainer) if a reference implementation is desired, but it is not required.
estimated_lines_of_code: 50-80 lines: ~30 lines for the RLOO gradient computation (sample k plays, compute leave-one-out baseline, compute weighted log-prob loss), ~20 lines for the training loop wrapper in a new src/actor_critic.py, and ~10-20 lines to wire into main_swarm.py as a new 'rl-train' subcommand.
transfer_learning_compatibility: Excellent. RLOO wraps the existing policy (SharedLotteryTransformer) and fine-tunes it with policy gradient updates. The pretrained encoder weights are used as initialization; only the output heads and optionally the top transformer layers need gradient updates. No architectural changes are required. The lottery_id embedding and per-lottery heads remain intact. RLOO is the most transfer-learning-friendly Actor-Critic alternative precisely because it adds no new network components (no critic head) — it only changes the loss computation.
specific_application_in_project: RLOO is the recommended Phase 2 Actor-Critic play generation method for lottery-nn. Concrete application: (1) For each historical draw date in draws_649.csv / draws_dailygrand.csv / draws.csv, generate k=6 candidate plays using the SharedLotteryTransformer with autoregressive masking. (2) Score each play against the actual draw result using semi-bandit number-level reward (count of matching numbers). (3) Compute the leave-one-out baseline for each play across the k=6 batch. (4) Update policy via -log_prob * advantage. This replaces the current temperature-softmax predict.py generation with a reward-driven policy that learns which ball distributions produce higher hit rates. Runs on the existing ~100-draw datasets per lottery without requiring a critic.
replaces_or_extends: Replaces temperature-softmax sampling in src/predict.py with a reward-driven REINFORCE policy. The SharedLotteryTransformer encoder and per-lottery heads are reused; only the generation and loss computation change. The Thompson sampling bandit in src/bandit.py continues to operate on top of RLOO-generated plays.
existing_open_source_implementations: 1. Hugging Face TRL library: trl.RLOOTrainer (official implementation, added in TRL v0.8+, designed for LLM RLHF but adaptable). 2. Original paper code: https://github.com/huggingface/trl/tree/main/trl/trainer (integrated into TRL). 3. Minimal standalone implementations exist in community repos (search 'RLOO REINFORCE leave one out pytorch' on GitHub). The algorithm is simple enough (~30 lines) that a from-scratch implementation is preferred for lottery-nn to avoid TRL's LLM-centric abstractions.
benchmark_results: Ahmadian et al. (2024): On Summarize from Feedback (Reddit TL;DR), RLOO with k=8 outperforms PPO (Actor-Critic) by 1-3 win-rate percentage points against the reference model as judged by GPT-4, while using 2x fewer GPU resources (no critic). On Anthropic HH dataset, RLOO matches or exceeds PPO at all scales tested (1B-7B parameters). Key finding: the learned critic in PPO introduces estimation error that RLOO avoids entirely. RLOO also outperforms single-sample REINFORCE by a significant margin (variance reduction from the leave-one-out baseline). RLOO with k=3 already matches PPO; k=8 exceeds it.
notable_use_cases: 1. RLHF alignment of language models (primary use case in Ahmadian et al.) — structurally similar to lottery in that reward is sparse (human preference labels) and dataset is finite. 2. Code generation RL fine-tuning: RLOO has been used to fine-tune code LLMs on unit-test pass/fail reward (binary sparse reward, similar to lottery hit/miss). 3. Mathematical reasoning (DeepSeek-R1 uses a REINFORCE-style multi-sample approach related to GRPO, a close relative of RLOO). 4. Combinatorial optimization via RL: pointer network training with REINFORCE leave-one-out baselines has been used for TSP and VRP (discrete combinatorial outputs, structurally analogous to selecting k numbers from {1..N}).
